title: Is the City Rail Link's ridership jump structural or a novelty effect? A preregistered prospective evaluation of rail uplift, bus substitution and job accessibility
hypothesis: Auckland's ratio of weekday (Tue-Thu, non-disrupted) rail to bus boardings held at 0.209-0.232 (monthly medians, Feb-Dec) from July 2023 to 10 September 2026, then jumped to about 0.307 (+37%) in the first full week after City Rail Link public services began on 13 September 2026. Hypothesis: over the confirmatory window 16 February - 25 March 2027 the ratio stays at least 20% above its pre-opening level for the same calendar window (ratio >= 0.27, one-sided 95% lower bound above +10%). That would mean at least ~55% of the opening-week uplift persists rather than fading as a novelty effect.
gap: The CRL (NZ$5.5b, New Zealand's largest transport project) opened on 11 September 2026. No independent after-the-fact evaluation exists. The only quantitative documents are AT's 2015 internal business case (forecasts made beforehand) and commentary. Three questions are open: does the opening jump persist (ramp-up vs novelty)? How much comes from people leaving buses rather than new trips? How is the timetable-based accessibility gain spread across Auckland? The window for a truly prospective evaluation, preregistered before the outcome data exist, closes within weeks.
value_rationale: Fills an actively discussed gap under unusually clean conditions: a single dated intervention, a highly stable control ratio (rail/bus within about 5% for three years), open counts updated weekly, and a preregistration made before the outcome data exist. That guards against after-the-fact spin in either direction on a NZ$5.5b project. Not 8+: outcomes are at line level, not station level, and a single city limits how far the result generalises.
cost_rationale: CPU-only with small data (<2 GB). r5py accessibility matrices for ~600 Auckland SA2s and two GTFS feeds take hours on 32 cores, and the ridership models are trivial. The main cost is calendar time (confirmatory data arrive around late March 2027), not compute. Optional GTFS-RT logging adds ~5-15 GB over 6 months.
est_wall_time: 2-3 days now (preregistration, counterfactual validation, accessibility analysis, a 6-week interim descriptive check), then ~1 day for the confirmatory test once AT publishes daily boardings through 25 March 2027 (~6 months calendar)

lit_for: Shinn & Voulgaris 2019, Transportation Research Record, 'Ridership Ramp-Up? Initial Ridership Variation on New Rail Transit Projects' (10.1177/0361198119844462): the basis for testing persistence vs novelty decay

Du, Huang & Zhou 2023, Cities, 'Impacts of a new urban rail transit line and its interactions with land use on the ridership of existing stations' (10.1016/j.cities.2023.104506): network effects of a new line

Greenaway-McGrevy 2024, Journal of Transport Economics and Policy, 'Mode Choice and the Effects of Rapid Transit Improvements on Private Vehicle Use and Urban Development' (10.3828/jtep.2024.58.1.1): an Auckland rapid-transit precedent

Javanmard, Liu & Long 2025, Travel Behaviour and Society, 'Using Realtime GTFS to generate easy-to-use transit accessibility measures under travel time uncertainty' (10.1016/j.tbs.2025.101054): method for the delivered-service accessibility arm
Braga, Loureiro & Pereira 2026, Journal of Transport Geography, travel-time variability, jobs competition and accessibility inequalities (10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2025.104526)

Skamris & Flyvbjerg 1997, Transport Policy, 'Inaccuracy of traffic forecasts and cost estimates on large transport projects' (10.1016/s0967-070x(97)00007-3): motivates an independent, preregistered evaluation after opening
lit_against: Novelty searches (Crossref 'City Rail Link' Auckland; Crossref Auckland rail accessibility/GTFS; arXiv Auckland AND transit/rail/bus; arXiv ridership AND accessibility AND rail/metro; arXiv new rail line/line opening ridership; the OpenAlex daily quota was exhausted mid-scan) found no evaluation of the CRL after opening. Crossref hits are construction/engineering papers, e.g., Galli, Ireland & Howard 2019/2020 on CRL land acquisition (10.1201/9780429424441-37)
Baker & Schloffel-Armstrong 2026, ''We can have beautiful things!' Why Auckland's City Rail Link is about much more than trains' (10.64628/aa.xgjhaj99h): commentary, with no quantitative evaluation
Auckland Transport's 2015 internal CRL business case (cityraillink.co.nz/crl-business-case): forecasts made before construction, not an evaluation

Lee, Boarnet & Houston 2017, Sustainability, 'Changes in Service and Associated Ridership Impacts near a New Light Rail Transit Line' (10.3390/su9101827): documents bus-to-rail reallocation, the substitution channel tested here in H2
method: Prospective, preregistered interrupted time series with a control series from within the same system. Primary outcome: the daily rail/bus boardings ratio on Tue-Thu non-disrupted days. Disruptions are flagged by rules frozen in the preregistration, using rail-replacement counts and ratio outliers. Counterfactual: the same-calendar-window ratio in 2024-2026, plus a regression/state-space model of the ratio on school-term, holiday and month effects, fitted to Jul 2023 - 10 Sep 2026. The null distribution of 'uplift' comes from 50+ placebo opening dates in the pre-period. The primary estimand is persistence: the Feb-Mar 2027 uplift relative to the opening-week uplift. Buses could lose riders to rail, which would inflate the ratio, so rail and bus boardings are also each modelled against their own seasonal baselines. Secondary H2: a route-level monthly difference-in-differences comparing bus routes whose GTFS shapes run within 800 m of the three new stations or along the isthmus/western corridors into the city centre with all other routes (Oct 2026 - Mar 2027 vs Oct 2025 - Mar 2026). The preregistered threshold is a relative loss of at least 5%. Secondary H3 (exploratory, constructive): timetable-based job accessibility from pre-CRL (Aug 2026) and post-CRL (Sep 2026) GTFS via r5py (jobs within 30/45/60 min, 7-9am median, weighted by SA2 population), mapped by area. With GTFS-RT logging, a delivered-service version (adjusted for cancellations and delays) tests how much of the timetabled gain survives day-to-day operations.
plan: Freeze and timestamp the preregistration before AT's next weekly data release: outcome definitions, disruption-flag rules, confirmatory window 16 Feb - 25 Mar 2027, thresholds and placebo design.

Assemble the AT daily and monthly-by-route series, flag disruption days, and fit and validate the counterfactual ratio model on Jul 2023 - 10 Sep 2026, using 50+ placebo openings to calibrate false-positive rates.

Download pre-CRL (Aug 2026) and post-CRL (Sep 2026) GTFS; build r5py networks on the OSM NZ extract; compute SA2-to-SA2 public-transport travel-time matrices (7-9am, 1-min departures) and maps of the change in job accessibility.
Classify bus routes by their exposure to the CRL corridor from GTFS shapes and stops, and prepare the route-level difference-in-differences for H2.
Optional: register for an AT API key and log GTFS-RT trip updates every 30 s to measure delivered rail service and cancellations through March 2027.
Publish a non-confirmatory 6-week interim descriptive update (no hypothesis test).

Once AT publishes data through 25 Mar 2027, run the confirmatory tests (H1 persistence, H2 substitution) and sensitivity analyses (bounds for transfer counting, separate rail and bus baselines, event days excluded), then write the report.
risks: (1) Counting artefact: AT boardings include train line-to-line transfers, and through-running lines change transfer patterns, so part of the uplift could be mechanical. This is handled by sensitivity bounds and reported explicitly, but cannot be fully separated using public data. (2) Concurrent changes (bus network or timetable changes, fare changes in Feb 2027, events, strikes, rail closures) can move the ratio; mitigated by disruption rules frozen in advance and separate baselines per mode. (3) If buses lose riders to rail, the ratio overstates the net rail effect; H2 measures this directly. (4) Pre-CRL GTFS needs a free Mobility Database account and GTFS-RT needs a free AT key. (5) The confirmatory result arrives only after ~6 months. Te Mana Raraunga: no Maori or individual-level data are used (aggregate counts, timetables, census totals). The station names were gifted by mana whenua. Any later equity analysis by ethnicity would use only published aggregates and be discussed with Maori data-governance experts first.
plain_summary: Auckland's City Rail Link tunnels opened to the public on 13 September 2026, and train trips jumped by about a third in the first week. This study writes down now, before the data exist, how big the lasting effect should be. In March 2027 it checks whether the jump held up or faded, and whether it came from new trips or from people leaving buses, giving Aucklanders an honest scorecard for a NZ$5.5 billion project.
local_relevance: Auckland Transport, Auckland Council, KiwiRail and the Ministry of Transport would get an independent, pre-committed estimate of the CRL's ridership effect and how many riders it drew from buses. They can use it to plan the bus network around the new stations, justify follow-on rail investment and benchmark future business cases.

title: What did reversing New Zealand's speed-limit cuts cost in crashes? A national difference-in-differences at road-segment level on the 2025 Setting of Speed Limits Rule reversals
hypothesis: The study covers road locations whose permanent posted limit was raised between 1 April and 31 October 2025. These are overwhelmingly reversals of post-2020 reductions under the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits 2024, mainly 80->100 km/h on rural roads and state highways and 30/40->50 km/h on urban streets. Hypothesis: police-reported injury crashes on these roads in the post-reversal period (FY2025/26 plus FY2026/27 to date) rose relative to matched locations whose limits did not change. The pooled difference-in-differences rate ratio is at least 1.10, with a one-sided 95% lower bound above 1.00.
gap: The 2024 Rule required road controlling authorities to reverse many 2020-2024 speed-limit reductions by 1 July 2025. The government argued the safety cost would be small; safety advocates predicted more deaths and serious injuries. No peer-reviewed or preprint evaluation of the reversals exists. Evidence on Auckland's own reductions is AT grey literature. The international literature is dominated by reductions (20 mph/30 km/h) or motorway increases, not by reversals of recent reductions on the same roads.
value_rationale: Directly informs a live national policy argument, and how NZTA and Auckland Transport apply the 2024 Rule and later amendments, with an independent estimate. Designs that reverse a cut on the same road are rare internationally, so the result also tests the symmetry assumption behind models linking speed to crash risk. Capped at 7 by limited power with one post-reversal year and coarse crash timing (financial year only).
cost_rationale: All data are open and under ~2 GB: CAS ~0.3 GB CSV, NSLR polygons <1 GB, OSM 0.4 GB, plus selected TMS count sites. Spatial joins and count models run in hours on CPU; no GPU.
est_wall_time: 2-3 days, plus a pre-committed re-run when FY2026/27 is complete (~Oct 2027), which roughly doubles post-period power

datasets.name: NZTA Crash Analysis System (CAS): all police-reported crashes with point locations (NZTM), severity, posted speed limit, crash year and financial year
datasets.access: open, CC BY 4.0, no account (FeatureServer or CSV download)

datasets.size: 56,000 zone polygons, <1 GB GeoJSON (subset of new limits Apr-Oct 2025: 4,095 polygons, 95 MB)

datasets.name: NZTA TMS daily traffic counts (state-highway exposure)
datasets.size: whole service ~11 GB; only affected sites are queried (<0.5 GB)

datasets.name: OpenStreetMap New Zealand extract (road network for segmentation and road class)

lit_for: Sayed & Sacchi 2016, Accident Analysis & Prevention, 'Evaluating the safety impact of increased speed limits on rural highways in British Columbia' (10.1016/j.aap.2016.07.012): crashes rose after limit increases; a before-after template with a comparison group
Brubacher et al. 2018, Sustainability, 'Road Safety Impact of Increased Rural Highway Speed Limits in British Columbia, Canada' (10.3390/su10103555)
Kokka et al. 2024, J Epidemiol Community Health, 'Effect of 20 mph speed limits on traffic injuries in Edinburgh, UK: a natural experiment and modelling study' (10.1136/jech-2023-221612)
Quddus, Theofilatos, Feng & Elvik 2025, Accident Analysis & Prevention, 'Evaluating the safety and speed impacts of the 20mph speed limit in the UK: Evidence and insights' (10.1016/j.aap.2025.108210)
Job & Brodie 2022, Journal of Road Safety, 'Understanding the role of Speeding and Speed in Serious Crash Trauma: A Case Study of New Zealand' (10.33492/jrs-d-21-00069)
Malyshkina & Mannering 2008, arXiv:0806.1354, 'Analysis of the Effect of Speed Limit Increases on Accident-Injury Severities'
arXiv:2408.00687 (2024), 'Reducing Urban Speed Limits Decreases Work-Related Traffic Injury Severity: Evidence from Santiago, Chile'
lit_against: No peer-reviewed or preprint evaluation of the 2025 New Zealand speed-limit reversals was found (searches: Europe PMC speed limit AND Auckland/New Zealand; Europe PMC speed limit reversal/increase AND crash/injury; Crossref Journal of Road Safety NZ/Auckland speed; arXiv speed limit AND crash/injury, speed limit AND increase/reversal, speed limit AND natural experiment; the OpenAlex daily quota was exhausted mid-scan)

Auckland Transport's own monitoring of its 2020-2023 Safe Speeds reductions (grey literature, not peer reviewed; figures not independently verified in this scan): covers the reductions, not the reversals
Mandic, Hewitt & Dodge 2023, Journal of Road Safety, 'Approaches to Managing Speed in New Zealand's Capital' (10.33492/jrs-d-22-00047): descriptive, with no causal crash estimate
Hu & Cicchino 2024, J Safety Research, 'Effects of lowering speed limits on crash severity in Seattle' (10.1016/j.jsr.2023.11.004): reductions only

Hunter et al. 2022, J Epidemiol Community Health, Belfast 20 mph 3-year follow-up (10.1136/jech-2022-219729): found little change in casualties, a caution that changing the posted limit may move actual speeds only slightly
method: Natural experiment analysed as a difference-in-differences at road-segment level. (i) Build a time-indexed speed-limit map: split OSM roads into ~100 m segments and assign the NSLR permanent limit in force on 1 May 2025 and 1 November 2025. Later snapshots are used to exclude locations changed again (e.g., 2026 school-zone or re-lowering changes). Changes are detected by comparing values at fixed dates, not by record end dates, because NSLR contains administrative re-certifications. (ii) Treated segments are those whose limit was raised in the window, grouped by transition type (rural 80->100; urban 30/40->50; other). The 100->110 expressway increases are analysed separately. Controls are unchanged segments matched (coarsened exact matching) on road controlling authority, urban/rural, prior limit history (reduced in 2020-24 and retained vs never reduced), road class and pre-period crash history. (iii) Snap CAS crashes to segments (<=30 m plus street-name agreement); the CAS speedLimit field serves as a manipulation check. (iv) Fit Poisson/negative-binomial difference-in-differences models with segment and stratum x financial-year fixed effects. Post period = FY2025/26 plus partial FY2026/27; the partial year is valid because treated and control segments share the same partial exposure. SEs are clustered by corridor/authority, with event-study pre-trends for FY2017/18-FY2024/25 and placebo reversal years. Secondary analyses: fatal+serious crashes, all crashes, the severity ratio, effects by transition type, state-highway models with TMS AADT exposure, and comparison with the Nilsson/Elvik power-model prediction for the observed limit changes. Pilot from this scan: 682 injury crashes (182 fatal or serious) in FY2023/24-FY2024/25 fell inside zones whose limit rose in Apr-Oct 2025. Most were on 80->100 (197) and 30->50 (158) transitions; 47% were on state highways and 20% in Auckland. That implies a minimum detectable effect of roughly 18-20% with one post-reversal year.
plan: Download CAS (FY2017/18 to present) and NSLR zones, snapshotting NSLR daily during the project to guard against silent edits.
Segment the OSM road network and assign the limits in force at 1 May 2025, 1 Nov 2025, 30 Jun 2026 and today; classify transitions and flag locations with other changes.

Snap crashes to segments; run the manipulation check (share of post-period crashes on treated segments recorded at the new limit) and data-quality filters that drop implausible transitions such as 10->50 or 50->100 polygon artefacts.
Match controls, estimate pre-trend event studies and placebo years, and report the minimum detectable effect before estimating any post-period effect.

Estimate the primary difference-in-differences rate ratio for injury crashes; then estimate fatal+serious, all-crash, severity and transition-specific effects, plus state-highway models with TMS exposure.
Robustness checks: alternative snapping tolerances, excluding school-zone segments, Auckland-only and state-highway-only subsets, and a spillover check on adjacent unchanged segments.
Write the report with tables aimed at NZTA and AT, and pre-commit to re-running once FY2026/27 data are complete.
risks: (1) Power: ~250-340 injury crashes per year on treated segments gives a minimum detectable effect near 18-20% with one post-reversal year, so a null result may be inconclusive; the CI will be reported and the analysis re-run in 2027. (2) Timing: public CAS gives only crash year and financial year, no dates. Reversals clustered around 1 July 2025 line up with the financial-year boundary, but staggered effective dates blur it. (3) Minor-injury and non-injury crashes from recent months are reported with a lag; this affects treated and control segments equally but adds noise. (4) NSLR history starts on 26 May 2022 and contains administrative re-certifications, so changes must be detected by comparing values at fixed dates. (5) Concurrent changes: mandatory variable school-zone limits (by July 2026), further 2026 changes (some Auckland zones were superseded again in Sept 2026), and shifts in enforcement and traffic volumes. (6) Selection: which reductions were reversed depended partly on community consultation outcomes. Te Mana Raraunga: CAS is non-personal and has no ethnicity field, so no Maori data are used. Maori are over-represented in road trauma; any later extension to ethnic disparities would require Maori-led governance of linked health data and is out of scope.
plain_summary: In 2025 the government made councils and NZTA raise many speed limits that had been lowered since 2020. This study compares crashes on roads where limits went back up with similar roads where nothing changed, to estimate how many extra injury crashes the reversal caused. That evidence matters for decisions about speed limits on Auckland's streets and the state highways around it.
local_relevance: NZTA, the Ministry of Transport and Auckland Transport, which manages many of the affected streets, can use the estimate in speed-management plans, the next Government Policy Statement on land transport and any future revision of the speed-limit rule.

title: Did the regulator's water-value model see the 2024 power-price crisis coming? A calibration audit of the Electricity Authority's weekly JADE simulations against actual wholesale prices, 2023-2025
hypothesis: The Electricity Authority published 103 weekly JADE runs (2023: 43, 2024: 33, 2025: 27). Hypothesis: the actual time-weighted average wholesale price at Haywards (HAY2201) in the first simulated week that lies wholly after the run's inputs were fixed (stage 2) exceeds the 90th percentile of JADE's simulated price distribution (91 historical inflow sequences) in at least 20% of runs, twice the nominal 10%. In addition, among runs starting with national hydro storage below its historical 20th percentile for that week, the exceedance rate is at least three times the rate in the other runs.
gap: Since 2023 the EA has published weekly runs of JADE as its benchmark for marginal water values. JADE is the open-source hydro-thermal scheduling model (stochastic dual dynamic programming, SDDP) developed at the University of Auckland's EPOC. The August 2024 crisis (weekly prices near $800/MWh) is central to the current debate over whether NZ wholesale prices reflect fundamentals, gas scarcity or market power. Nobody has checked whether these simulations are calibrated against what actually happened. The closest work (Poletti 2020) measured market power for 2010-2016 with a different benchmark. A recent EA weekly monitoring report checked here compares prices with historical percentiles and does not reference JADE.
value_rationale: Fills an actively discussed but technical gap. Whether the official benchmark is calibrated, or demonstrably miscalibrated, matters for EA market monitoring, security-of-supply assessments and the gentailer/market-power debate that sets the power prices Auckland households and businesses pay. Kept at 6 because calibration failure alone cannot separate market power from risk aversion or from mis-modelled gas constraints; the secondary analyses address this only partially.
cost_rationale: CPU-only, a few days. The work streams ~9 GB of JADE outputs and ~95 GB of offers (filtered on the fly to hydro units, ~3 GB kept) plus 0.4 GB of prices; the analysis itself is light. Optional JADE.jl re-runs with the open HiGHS solver for 4-6 crisis weeks take hours each on 32 cores.
est_wall_time: 4-6 days (1 day download/filter, 2 days calibration analysis, 1-2 days offer-markup secondary analysis; +1-2 days for optional JADE re-runs)

datasets.name: Electricity Authority EMI 'Expected water values': weekly JADE runs, inputs and outputs, including tidy_results with simulated prices at NI/SI/HAY, marginal water values by reservoir and reservoir levels (91 inflow sequences x 52 stages)
datasets.size: 103 runs with tidy_results = 9.1 GB; full folders 31 GB

datasets.name: EMI final energy prices, half-hourly by node (monthly files)
EMI generator offers by unit, tranche and trading period (daily files)
datasets.size: 2023 10.1 GB, 2024 19.1 GB, 2025 65.9 GB (filtered while streaming to hydro energy offers, ~3 GB kept)

datasets.name: EMI Hydrological Modelling Dataset (daily storage, spill and flows for major reservoirs, to 31 Dec 2024)
JADE.jl source code (EPOC, University of Auckland)
datasets.access: open source (custom licence; check terms before redistribution); HiGHS solver is open

lit_for: Hole, Philpott & Dowson 2024, European Journal of Operational Research, 'Capacity planning of renewable energy systems using stochastic dual dynamic programming' (10.1016/j.ejor.2024.12.031): the SDDP/JADE lineage at EPOC, University of Auckland
Pritchard 2015, European Journal of Operational Research, 'Stochastic inflow modeling for hydropower scheduling problems' (10.1016/j.ejor.2015.05.022)

arXiv:2607.00504 (2026), 'How optimistic inflow forecasts distort dispatch, prices, and contracts in hydro-dominated power systems: evidence from Brazil': the closest analogue (bias in an official hydro-scheduling model)
Leclere & Philpott 2025, Operations Research Letters, 'Strategic behavior of risk-averse agents under stochastic market clearing' (10.1016/j.orl.2025.107365)
Philpott, Read & Batstone 2019, IEEE Power and Energy Magazine, 'The New Zealand Electricity Market: Challenges of a Renewable Energy System' (10.1109/mpe.2018.2871705)
lit_against: Poletti 2020, Energy Economics, 'Market Power in the New Zealand electricity wholesale market 2010-2016' (10.1016/j.eneco.2020.105078): the closest study using a market-power benchmark; it pre-dates JADE EWV and the gas-constrained 2023-2025 period

Hassan, Prasad & Kilby 2026, Energies, 'State-Dependent Merit-Order Effects in a Hydro-Dominated Market ... New Zealand' (10.3390/en19163747): models how price depends on storage and thermal share, but does not evaluate JADE forecasts

Young, Poletti & Browne 2014, Energy Economics, 'Can agent-based models forecast spot prices in electricity markets? Evidence from the New Zealand electricity market' (10.1016/j.eneco.2014.08.007): evaluated price forecasts from a different (agent-based) model
Browne, Poletti & Young 2012, New Zealand Economic Papers, 'Simulating market power in the New Zealand electricity market' (10.1080/00779954.2011.649566)

Electricity Authority weekly trading-conduct reports and half-yearly structure-conduct-performance reviews (grey literature): they monitor prices against historical percentiles; the 14-20 June 2026 report checked here does not reference JADE water values, and no published calibration of EWV was found (searches: OpenAlex NZ market power / water values / SDDP NZ / DOASA; Crossref Jade expected water values; arXiv NZ electricity AND hydro/water value/wholesale, water values AND SDDP AND price, water value AND hydropower AND forecast/calibration)
method: Calibration audit of an official stochastic model's forecasts. For each weekly run, extract the stage-1 and stage-2 simulated prices (91 historical inflow sequences) at HAY, NI and SI, and combine block prices into time-weighted weekly averages using that run's hours_per_block. Compute actual time-weighted weekly averages at HAY2201, BEN2201 and OTA2201 (Otahuhu, Auckland's reference node) over the matching JADE weeks (week 1 starts on 1 January). Primary test: how often stage 2 exceeds the simulated 90th percentile. Stage 2 is used because run inputs are dated day 2 of the JADE week, so stage 1 is partly elapsed. CIs come from a moving-block bootstrap to handle autocorrelation. Storage state comes from run-start reservoir levels, converted to national energy-storage percentiles using the EMI hydrological dataset. Secondary analyses: (a) PIT histograms and coverage of 50/80/90% intervals at horizons 1-4; (b) CRPS skill against climatology and persistence; (c) regression of log(actual/JADE median) on storage percentile, HVDC/thermal outages and gas-price inputs; (d) hydro offer markups, i.e. the price of the marginal cleared hydro tranche relative to the stage-1 marginal water value of its reservoir, by storage state and firm. Optional constructive arm: re-run JADE.jl with HiGHS for the worst-calibrated weeks under (a) CVaR risk aversion and (b) gas-constrained thermal availability, to see which assumption closes the gap. Pilot fact from this scan: the run for 2024 week 32 (inputs dated 6 Aug 2024) simulated Haywards PEAK-block prices of $237/$294/$344 per MWh at p10/p50/p90. The actual average for 5-11 Aug 2024 was $797/MWh (Benmore $805).
plan: List and download the tidy_results of all 103 runs, filtering to price, mwv, reslevel and total_storage rows on the fly, plus hours_per_block and the run timestamps.
Download the 2023-2025 monthly final-price files and build actual weekly time-weighted prices at HAY2201, BEN2201 and OTA2201 aligned to JADE weeks.
Construct a storage percentile for each run start from the EMI hydrological dataset history and the JADE stage-0 reservoir levels.
Freeze the analysis plan; compute PIT, coverage, exceedance rates and CRPS skill by horizon; run the primary exceedance test and the storage-ratio test with a block bootstrap.
Filter the 2023-2025 offers to hydro units while streaming; compute marginal-tranche markups over reservoir marginal water values and relate them to storage and firm.
Optional: re-run JADE.jl with HiGHS for 4-6 crisis weeks under risk-averse and gas-constrained variants.
Write the report with recommendations for the EA (e.g., publish calibration diagnostics alongside the weekly EWV).
risks: (1) JADE runs are policy simulations (risk-neutral, historical inflow sequences, fixed demand), not designed as price forecasts, so miscalibration may reflect intended simplifications; results are framed as an audit of the benchmark, not a model 'failure'. (2) Small effective sample: 103 autocorrelated weeks, with the crisis concentrated in roughly 10 of them. The series has gaps (weeks 4-9 of 2024 and 2025, and late-year weeks) and ends at 2025 week 34. (3) Mapping between JADE (nodes NI, SI, HAY; PEAK/SHOULDER/OFFPEAK blocks) and half-hourly nodal prices is approximate; time-weighted weekly averages reduce this. (4) Calibration alone cannot separate market power, risk aversion and mis-modelled gas supply. (5) Offer files are large (2025: 66 GB), so they are filtered while streaming and never stored raw. Te Mana Raraunga: the hydro schemes sit on awa subject to Treaty settlements (e.g., Waikato River, Waitaki). The study uses only market and hydrological data, no Maori data, and makes no claims about iwi interests.
plain_summary: New Zealand's electricity regulator runs a computer model every week to estimate how valuable the water in hydro lakes is, and uses that as a benchmark for whether power prices are fair. This study checks the model against what actually happened in 2023-2025. For example, in one week of the August 2024 crisis the model's middle price was under $300/MWh even for the busiest hours, but actual prices averaged nearly $800. Knowing when and why the benchmark misses matters for every Auckland household and business whose power price tracks the wholesale market.
local_relevance: The Electricity Authority's market-monitoring team, MBIE's energy-security work and EPOC at the University of Auckland (JADE's developers) could use the calibration diagnostics to improve the weekly water-value benchmark and to judge future price spikes. Large Auckland electricity users and consumer advocates would gain an independent read on whether scarcity prices reflected fundamentals.
